dropped_turns.text: Would you deny a threatened village any organized defense while it waits for distant approval? No, because people may protect themselves when danger is immediate and plainly real.

Keep responses direct, and let the other speaker finish.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Hezbollah could not claim the authority of an entire country simply by acting in its name. War places every family at risk, so only accountable national institutions can make that choice. A party with its own fighters cannot substitute itself for Lebanon. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: So, let's let Greg jump in. Okay.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The question is not whether every decision made in war was wise. It is whether people facing attack may defend their communities when their state cannot protect them. A movement rooted among those communities can resist aggression and express a real demand for safety. Denying that role ignores the people who depend on it.

turns.text: I can give you ten seconds to wrap this round.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I agree that communities need protection when institutions fail. But protection is not a blank check to launch war for everyone; consent needs a lawful national decision before combat.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Where a state truly cannot defend people under attack, community resistance may have legitimacy. In that situation, waiting for permission can leave families defenseless and abandons their right to safety.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: War also leaves ruined homes, displaced children, and bitter memories that last beyond any ceasefire. But the motion is authority: Hezbollah could not appoint itself to decide Lebanon's fate.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: People do not lose the right to resist merely because institutions are imperfect. Does a community's right of self-defense vanish while officials fail to act?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No, people retain a right to safety, but that does not give one faction the right to speak for all of them. Self-defense belongs to people, not an unaccountable force claiming Lebanon.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Disarmament cannot be imposed by simply collecting weapons and calling that peace. It requires guarantees, local trust, and protection against future attacks; otherwise, civilians are left exposed.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: We're talking about whether hezbollah had the right to fight on Lebanon's behalf.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Resistance always deserves a voice. When people face danger, silencing those who organize defense treats them as spectators rather than citizens with a stake in survival and dignity.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Who gave Hezbollah permission to expose every Lebanese household to retaliation? You cannot point to a national decision, because none was secured before it claimed that immense power for Lebanon.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: This hostage-taking resistance does not deserve a voice. Yet its broader claim to defend communities shows why rejecting all resistance would deny people any means of survival in a crisis.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Yes, a cause differs from its spokesman, but neither gives a faction authority to choose war for Lebanon. Your distinction still leaves ordinary people without a say in the decision.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Imagine a border village under attack while officials issue speeches and no protection arrives. Local defenders repel the assault and families remain; that proves resistance can exercise a necessary right.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I grant that abandoned villages need immediate defense. But immediate defense is not authority to widen a war, define a nation, and accept suffering for people who never chose you.
